draft.title: Finding trends in economic data
card: A trend is the general direction data moves over time. It can be rising, falling or steady.
Look at the first and last points in a period, then check the points in between. A line graph helps you see the overall direction.
A trend can still hold when some years go against it. One year that dips does not cancel a rise over five years.
A longer period gives a better picture than one or two data points. Name the direction and the time period when you describe a trend.
draft.remember: A trend is the overall direction over a period, not what happens in one year.

a.q: Which statement describes a trend in this data? Bread prices: Year 1 $3.00, Year 2 $3.20, Year 3 $3.10, Year 4 $3.40, Year 5 $3.60.
opts: Bread prices rose over the five years
Bread prices fell in Year 3, so prices fell
Bread prices were steady over the five years
Bread prices were $3.20 in Year 2
a.why: Prices went from $3.00 to $3.60 over the five years, so the overall direction is up. The fall in Year 3 is only one year going against the trend, and it does not change the general direction.
a.clue: Look at the whole period, not one year.

b.q: Sam tracks the weekly price of a bus ticket in Hobart: $4.00, $4.10, $4.20, $4.30, $4.20, $4.40. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
opts: The trend is rising, with one small fall in week 5
The trend is falling, because week 5 was lower
There is no trend, because one week fell
The trend is steady, because prices are close
b.why: The price rose from $4.00 to $4.40 over six weeks, so the general direction is up. The week 5 fall is one point going against the trend. It is not enough to say the trend is falling or that there is no trend.
b.clue: Compare the start and end, then ask if one dip changes the direction.

a.best: Bread prices rose over the five years

b.best: The trend is rising, with one small fall in week 5

problems.detail: Bus fares in Hobart (Metro Tasmania) are set by government and do not change from week to week, so a weekly-changing ticket price is an unrealistic example. Something like weekly petrol prices would be more believable.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear correct answer that matches the card and the explanations. The only issue is that Question b uses a Hobart bus fare that changes every week, which is unrealistic and could be swapped for something like petrol prices.

flags: Question b, fact: Bus fares in Hobart (Metro Tasmania) are set by government and do not change from week to week, so a weekly-changing ticket price is an unrealistic example. Something like weekly petrol prices would be more believable.
